solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: the colon clause ('nearly every roadside, fence line and riverbank') defines the word almost directly; A/B are clearly wrong, so it comes down to C vs D
S033-01.notes: 'Grows along nearly every roadside...' = found everywhere -> ubiquitous. 'Ornamental' echoes 'gardens', but the change described is about how widespread it is, not what it's used for. 'Endangered' and 'dormant' contradict the spread.

flags: minor: 'finished' is the direct opposite and 'conventional'/'extravagant' have no support, so the item is easy to eliminate down to A
S033-02.notes: Leaving land unbuilt and roads extendable so buildings can be added later = open-ended. 'Finished' is the opposite; nothing suggests the plan was lavish or ordinary.

flags: minor: simplified science. Cassini found silica nanoparticles (in E-ring grains fed by the plumes; Hsu et al. 2015) and read them as evidence of hydrothermal activity, roughly >90 C water in contact with rock. The claim 'hot enough to dissolve rock' loosely means 'dissolve silica from rock'; acceptable for the SAT level
S033-03.notes: The grains form where hot water dissolves rock and then cools -> water under the surface is heated in contact with rock. A (meteorites) ignores the Earth analogy. C contradicts 'plumes of water vapor'. D is about the surface, which the text doesn't address.

S033-04.notes: If the snail still withdraws at once from a new kind of touch, it can still withdraw, so it isn't tired; it has stopped responding only to the familiar harmless tap (stimulus specificity in habituation). B points toward fatigue. A fits both explanations equally (faster tapping could also tire it faster). D only repeats the starting behavior. A is the main distractor for quick readers.

flags: minor: the key is the longest choice and the only one that compares against the no-lamp baseline, which may tip off careful test-takers
S033-05.notes: Extra insects over the baseline: amber 45-10=35, white 120-10=110. That is a reduction of about 68% ('greatly reduce'), and 35>0 means 'not eliminate'. B only shows that white is highest and doesn't address 'not eliminate' or the size of the drop. C and D each give a single value. B is the trap.

flags: minor: Text 2 never states its view on climate outright. D rests on the inference that 'less able to withstand hard years' grants the hard conditions. That inference is reasonable, and D is hedged ('may have mattered alongside')
minor: historically accurate. Norse Greenland lasted c. 985 to the early-to-mid 1400s, and the walrus-ivory trade decline is a current scholarly hypothesis (e.g., Barrett, Star et al.)
S033-06.notes: Text 2 adds an economic factor (falling ivory trade) that made the settlements vulnerable to hard years. It doesn't deny the cooling, so it would see trade loss as mattering alongside climate. A goes too far. B misreads the text: demand fell, not the ability to hunt. C contradicts Text 2's added factor.

flags: minor: answer cue. B is the only choice that gives a reason ('Because...'), and D states the conclusion without the evidence, so the item is quick to eliminate down to B
minor: facts check out (June 30, 1908; ~80 million trees; ~2,150 km2; Kulik expedition 1927; no impact crater)
S033-07.notes: The goal is to explain why scientists think it was an airburst. Only B links the evidence (wide damage but no crater) to the conclusion. D gives the conclusion with no reason; A and C give background only.

S033-08.notes: The second sentence gives specific design features that carry out the energy-saving claim -> 'Specifically'. There is no contrast, so A and B are out. 'Previously' clashes with the present-tense description of the new building.

flags: minor: facts check out. A living coelacanth was identified off East London, South Africa, in 1938, and the group had been thought extinct since the end of the Cretaceous
S033-09.notes: The appositive closes with an em dash ('dinosaurs—was'), so it must open with an em dash too. A comma (A) mixes punctuation. A semicolon (B) splits the subject from the verb. No punctuation (C) leaves the closing dash unpaired. The comma is the common trap.

flags: minor: 'their' for a collective noun like 'council' is accepted in British and informal usage, but SAT convention treats it as singular, so A is the standard key
S033-10.notes: The antecedent is 'the city council' (singular collective), and a possessive is needed -> 'its'. 'It's' and 'they're' are contractions, and 'their' is plural. The trap is 'their' (council members).
